author: syntaxwanderer
body:
## Summary

An `#[ExternalApi]` route promises a machine-facing envelope, and a validation failure was the one error it never got one for.

The mapper was not missing. `ExternalApiExceptionMapper` already answers a `ValidationException`, and its own test pins the shape. It was never **asked**: `RouteExecutor` built the flat 422 itself and returned it from the hydrate/validate stage, before any `ExceptionResponseMapperInterface` was reached.

## Changes

The stage now names **what** went wrong and leaves the shape to the mapper. All three rejection points — a `ValidationException` from `validate()`, a type mismatch, and an unparseable body — become a `PayloadValidationException`, which the outer catch maps and decorates exactly as the early return did.

**The type is the whole design.** A handler throwing `ValidationException` states a *domain rule* and keeps the `{error, message, context}` envelope; the same class raised in the pipeline means the request was *malformed* and has always answered with the flat `{errors: {field: [message]}}`. **Eleven test files depend on that flat shape**, so a plain rethrow would have changed it for every one of them.

The task that proposed this listed three options and called this one the largest. It is the smallest: `ExceptionResponseMapperInterface` already lives in core, `ResolvedRouteMetadata` already carries the `external_api` flag, and `RouteExecutor` already resolves the mapper. Nothing new crosses the package boundary.

## Checks

- `composer phpstan` — 177, unchanged
- `bin/semitexa test:run` — 8416 PHPUnit + 97 E2E green

## What to review

**The generic `\Throwable` catch does not chain the original exception.** A hydration crash still surfaces as a 422 with `_body` and the cause discarded — identical to before, so not a regression, but now that it flows through the mapper a `previous` would be naturally loggable. Left out to keep the change to one idea; worth a second opinion on whether it belongs here.

I checked the one thing that could have silently changed behaviour: the outer catch **rethrows** when the mapper or metadata is null, where the old code returned 422 regardless. Both are resolved at line 123, long before validation runs at 171, and `resolveExceptionMapper()` has a non-nullable return type — so that branch is unreachable from here.

## What to verify

A non-external route's 422 body is byte-identical; an `#[ExternalApi]` route now gets the envelope; a handler-thrown `ValidationException` is unchanged on both. All three are pinned in `PayloadValidationEnvelopeTest`.

One observable change: the stage no longer marks `request.short_circuit`. The outer catch marks `request.exception` with the class and then `request.exception.mapped` with the status, so a trace reader learns strictly more.

author: burbanit0
body:
## Summary

**Live break on `develop` right now** — confirmed via `develop`'s own post-merge push run (E2E Tests, run 34801385716: "completed failure"), not something introduced by an unrelated PR.

PR #469 (a Dependabot grouped patch-and-minor bump) bumped `@playwright/test` 1.62.1 → 1.63.0, but the `visual-regression` job's pinned Docker image tag (`mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.62.1-noble`) is a separate, manually-maintained string that Dependabot's npm ecosystem never touches. Result: every run since fails immediately with `Executable doesn't exist at /ms-playwright/chromium_headless_shell-1243/...` and Playwright's own error message explaining exactly why.

## Fix

Bumped the pin to `v1.63.0-noble`, matching `@playwright/test` exactly. Verified for real: pulled the new image and confirmed `/ms-playwright/` contains `chromium_headless_shell-1243` — the exact executable the old image was missing.

## Review

Ran `/code-review ultra` (touches a CI/CD workflow). It raised a real, worth-checking concern: bumping the Docker image also bumps the underlying browser engines (Chromium 151→153 per Playwright's browsers.json), and the 7 committed screenshot baselines were never regenerated against the new renderer — with zero pixel tolerance configured, that's a plausible break. Checked for real rather than assumed either way: regenerated all 7 baselines inside the new image (`scripts/test-visual-docker.sh --update-snapshots`) and diffed against what's committed — **byte-identical, zero git diff**. Confirmed with a second, non-update run against the existing baselines: 7/7 pass. No snapshot update needed.

Also fixed a second finding: `.claude/skills/voter-ci/SKILL.md` hardcoded the old tag in prose, which would've gone stale the instant this PR's own bump landed. Rewritten to point at `e2e.yml` as the source of truth instead of repeating a number that's meant to move.

## Test plan

- [x] Confirmed live break via `develop`'s own push-triggered E2E run (not merely reproduced on a branch)
- [x] Pulled `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.63.0-noble` directly and confirmed `chromium_headless_shell-1243` is present
- [x] Regenerated all 7 visual-regression baselines inside the new image — byte-identical to committed baselines (zero diff)
- [x] Re-ran the suite in compare mode (no `--update-snapshots`) against the existing committed baselines using the new image — 7/7 pass
- [x] YAML validated
- [x] `/code-review ultra` — one concern raised, checked for real, confirmed not an issue; one doc staleness found and fixed

author: lucifron28
camoa
body:
Works the six proposals dated 2026-09-14: the two live-run findings appended to `surfaces-recipe-ask.md`, `surfaces-narrowing-token-ask.md`, `worktree-environment-ask.md`, its follow-ups `worktree-environment-tokens-ask.md` and `worktree-environment-tokens-finding.md`, and the count question in `playbook-sets-ask.md`.

## The two surfaces findings (`af49997`, `5e35b00`)

- **Discovery no longer assumes `web/`.** `visual-regression-setup.md` (0.3.1) says how to find the docroot and the configuration sync folder: `composer.json` installer paths or `ddev drush status --field=root`, and `$settings['config_sync_directory']` or `ddev drush status --field=config-sync`. The default theme comes from `system.theme.yml` in that folder. `e2e-setup-atk.md` (0.2.1) names the sync folder the same way. Its three `cp -R web/modules/contrib/...` install lines still assume `web/`, and its Preconditions say so; a line cannot vary, so a project with another docroot cannot run that install through the plugin.
- **The `e2e` row has one marker.** The plugin reads every code span in a `silent_pass` text as a marker and matches by substring, so `chromium` fired on every run and `1 passed` would have fired on `11 passed`. The spec the e2e recipe writes now prints `no e2e surface is enabled` once, at collection, when nothing is enabled; that line is the row's only code span. Checked through the plugin's own parser: one marker on `e2e`, none on the other five rows. A spec installed by 0.2.0 lacks the line and is never overwritten; the recipe says a person adds it.
- The marker rule itself was enforced by the plugin and stated nowhere in the catalog. It is now one sentence in the index's surface-commands paragraph.

## The narrowing token (`cd7908f`)

`checks.md` (0.5.0): the `e2e` and `visual-regression` rows carry `--grep {surfaces}` like the accept row. On Playwright 1.63.0, `--grep` on the `chromium` project leaves the `setup` dependency in the run, so preflight and QA login still happen; a fill that matches no title prints `Error: No tests found` and exits 1 before any project runs. Both facts are on the row.

## The worktree-environment recipe (`b653d21`)

New capability `worktree-environment`, one recipe, `drupal/worktree-environment.md` (0.1.0 in this commit, 0.2.1 by the end of the branch), with the sections the plugin reads: `## Preconditions`, `## Bring up`, `## Address`, `## Tear down`, `## Build in place`. The index gains the recipe row, the type row, the declaration row and the contract paragraph.

It follows DDEV's documented worktree workflow and links the pages rather than restating them. It departs from the proposal in three places, each forced by running it:

1. **The worktree is a sibling of the checkout, not `<codePath>/.claude/worktrees/<id>`.** DDEV hands an unregistered nested project to the nearest registered ancestor. Only an interactive `ddev start` asks `Use the nested project?`; `-y` keeps the outer project, and no global setting or environment variable changes that (`pkg/ddevapp/nested_project.go`). In the nested layout, every unnamed command reached the main site, and a repeated tear-down deleted the main project's containers and database volume with exit 0. Beside the checkout, the same commands registered the worktree's own project on the first non-interactive try. **The task skill's worktree path has to change for DDEV projects**, or bring-up cannot be automated.
2. **Three tokens, not `{codePath}`.** DDEV addresses a project by name and never by path, and the catalog substitutes a placeholder only as a whole token. `{mainProject}` and `{mainFiles}` come from DDEV's project list; the worktree's project name comes from the address at bring-up and names the project on tear-down, so a repeat can never land on another project.
3. **`## Address` runs between two `## Bring up` blocks.** Its `.raw.approot` must be the worktree before anything seeds a database. The index paragraph states this as the contract.

Seeding uses DDEV's own worktree support: `ddev snapshot <main>` then `ddev snapshot restore --latest` in the worktree, no file copied. The snapshot carries no `--name`, because a second snapshot under an existing name is refused with exit 0 and a fixed name would restore a stale seed silently; each bring-up leaves one timestamped snapshot in the main checkout's `.ddev/db_snapshots/`, and the recipe says so.

Observed end to end on a fresh Drupal 11.4 standard site, DDEV 1.25.4, every command run without a terminal: two projects with distinct addresses, the site name across, `HTTP/2 200` at the worktree, a file served at one address and 404 at the other, a clean tree in both checkouts, tear-down by name safe to repeat. A first draft that used export and import and the nested layout failed on both counts; those runs are what produced the three departures. The plugin-side notes are in the aida-v6 project's handoff document.

## The tokens ask and its finding (`0e84014`, `b52650e`)

Recipe 0.2.1 takes the follow-up ask as written, so the plugin holds no DDEV command. A `## Tokens` section: one `sh` block per token, the token's name as the fence's second word, one command, `{codePath}` as a whole argument; the first stdout line is the value, and nothing printed or a non-zero exit refuses by the token's name. `## Files` writes three scripts under `.aida/environment/` that hold every `ddev` and `jq` call. `## Address` runs one of them and prints `address:`, `project:` and `root:`; `root:` is the guard, and `project:` fills `{project}` for the tear-down (the finding: the plugin fills a token under the key the address printed, so 0.2.0's `{worktreeProject}` was a name nothing filled). Two `## Bring up` headings sit around `## Address`, read in document order, said once in the Goal.

Run end to end again on a fresh Drupal 11.4 site: the token scripts printed their values, and nothing with exit 4 for a path that is no project; the address printed the worktree as root; both bring-up blocks and the tear-down exited 0, twice. That run also showed the three written scripts left untracked fail the clean-tree check and make `git worktree remove` refuse with exit 128, so committing them on the task's branch is now an explicit step on the yes path; the Verifier says a run with that commit made is not yet observed.

## The playbook count

`llms.txt` says 29 guides for `drupal/best-practices/camoa` and `plays.json` holds 28. The extra one is `sources-maintenance.md`, not `index.md`: `generate_llms.py` counts every `*.md` except `index.md`, for every topic, and the plays manifest also drops the maintenance record. That is a catalog-wide counting convention, so it is reported here and not changed.

## Checks

`validate_recipes.py`: 43 valid. `pytest tests/`: 17 passed. `check_publish_invariants.py`: no new violations. The strict build runs in CI. A fresh verifier read the recipe, the index diff and the two run reports against the proposals; its twelve findings are fixed in `b653d21`, except the claims it could not check because it lacked the run artifacts (the Playwright `--grep` runs and the `drush status` fields), which were run in the session.

author: google-labs-jules[bot]
body:
🛡️ Sentinel Security Fix: Transmit Gemini API key in `x-goog-api-key` HTTP header.

### 🚨 Severity
HIGH

### 💡 Vulnerability
The direct Gemini REST request in `src/services/geminiGateway.ts` included the sensitive API key as a URL query parameter (`?key=${activeKey}`).

### 🎯 Impact
Transmitting API keys via URL query strings can leak sensitive credentials in web server logs, proxy logs, network monitoring tools, and browser history.

### 🔧 Fix
Updated `src/services/geminiGateway.ts` to omit the `key` query parameter from the request URL and instead pass `x-goog-api-key: activeKey` in the request headers.

### ✅ Verification
Ran `pnpm lint` and `pnpm build` to confirm TypeScript compilation and build success with zero errors.

Dynamo recorded a stream's tracing-rank device and guarded stream inputs by
their exact identity. Reusing a compile_on_one_rank artifact on another rank
could therefore expose the original device index or recompile even when the
same current-stream relationship held.

Carry runtime-relative device provenance through stream variables and guard
stream equality by whether the input is the current stream. Normalize default,
indexless, and negative-device constructors while leaving fixed and CPU devices
unchanged.

body:
## Summary

The blunder page's board now shows the move that was played as arrows, read from the stored notation. The arrows are static: always the played move, never a selectable candidate.

- **Notation** — `parseMove` in `@repo/core` turns `13/9(3) 6/2*`, `bar/22*/17*` or `3/off(2)` into one move per checker. `BAR_PIP` (25) is the bar and `OFF_PIP` (0) is off, so `from - to` is always the pips travelled. A chain is one move per stop, and a repeat hits only on its first checker.
- **Arrows** — `Board` takes a `move` prop, drawn by `MoveArrows`: one straight red arrow per checker, with a cream casing so it reads over dark checkers and points.
- **Where arrows start** — at the edge of the moving checker, or its middle when checkers on neighbouring points leave no room for a line.
- **Where arrows end** — at the edge of a checker already drawn at the landing spot (a hit blot, or the top of an overflowing stack), otherwise at the middle of the empty spot or tray slot.
- **Several checkers** — stacks are replayed through the play, so each checker leaves a different drawn checker. Repeated journeys are paired so their arrows run parallel instead of crossing.

## The side on roll

The page now passes `turn="player"` instead of the XGID's turn field. gnubg lays out every position for the side on roll, so that side is always the near one, but the stored turn field is -1 on 980 of 1,380 positions. Until now that drew the dice in the far half on those boards, and it would have drawn the arrows for the wrong side.

## Verification

- `pnpm --filter @repo/core verify` now replays all 3,946 candidate plays from the near side of their source position (a checker on every stop left, hits only on single blots, no landing on a made point) and compares each result with Galaxy's own after-move XGID. All 3,946 match, and all 1,380 positions still agree with their GNU BG ids.
- `check-types`, `lint` and `format:check` pass.
- Rendered boards were screenshotted in headless Chrome for real positions covering: a bar entry hitting twice (`bar/22*/17*`), bearing off (`4/off(2)`), `bar/19(2) 8/2(2)`, a hit mid-move (`11/5*/3`), three checkers off a six-stack (`bar/22 13/10(3)`), `18/16(3) 10/8`, `bar/24 8/7*(2) 6/5`, and `24/23 24/20`.

## Noted, not addressed

- The copyable XGID still carries that turn field, so pasting it into XG puts the wrong side on roll. The fix belongs in the scraper's `toXgid`, whose comment assumes every Galaxy position has gnubg turn 1. That holds for after-move positions but not for the positions blunders were made in.
- A straight arrow along a row passes over any checkers between its ends, e.g. `24/20` on blunder 16801764.

Closes BG-21

author: ocavue
body:
Reflect Capture updates currently require a manual version bump and Chrome Web Store upload. This adds an independent draft extension Release PR: marking it ready and merging it publishes a GitHub release with an `extension-vX.Y.Z` tag and calls **Release Browser Extension**, which builds the ZIP from that commit and submits it using the standard `wxt submit` command. Google publishes the update after review approval.

- Keeps desktop beta/stable versions separate. All three release-please configurations open draft PRs; release-please publishes extension GitHub releases directly.
- Uses one job to install dependencies, build the ZIP, and submit it with WXT.
- Renames the desktop workflow to **Release App** (`release-app.yml`) and updates callers and existing tests.
- Shares Node.js 22/pnpm setup and frozen-lockfile dependency installation through `.github/actions/setup-node` across the CI and release workflows.
- Updates release instructions and capture privacy text for the existing X bookmark observer.

### Maintainer setup before merging an extension Release PR

No credentials were generated, no store uploads were made, and no GitHub secrets/settings were changed by this PR.

1. In [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/), select/create a project and enable **Chrome Web Store API**.
2. Under **IAM & Admin → Service Accounts**, create a publisher service account, or reuse the one already linked to your Chrome publisher. Broad Google Cloud project roles are not needed.
3. In the [Chrome Web Store Developer Dashboard](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole), open the publisher that owns item `ccabifmooehighoonjeiololjfofkhkd`. Under **Account**, link the service-account email. Only one service account can be linked per publisher; check existing configuration first.
4. Create/download a JSON key for that service account. Copy its `client_email` and `private_key` values into GitHub repository **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**:

   | Secret | Value |
   | --- | --- |
   | `CHROME_PUBLISHER_ID` | Publisher ID from the Developer Dashboard, not the extension item ID |
   | `CHROME_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_CLIENT_EMAIL` | JSON key's `client_email` |
   | `CHROME_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_PRIVATE_KEY` | JSON key's `private_key`, as the PEM block with real newlines |

   Follow [Google's service-account instructions](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/service-accounts). There is no need to run `wxt submit init`, generate a user OAuth refresh token, or configure an OAuth consent screen. Do not commit the JSON key or `.env.submit`.
5. The existing release-please workflow uses `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Ensure Actions may create pull requests under **Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions**, as required by the existing desktop release process. The workflows declare the required contents and pull-request permissions.
6. Before the first store submission, confirm the current published/pending version, account 2-step verification, and listing/privacy declarations, including `webRequest`, `https://x.com/*`, and the default-enabled X bookmark capture. Verify the extension against the supported installed desktop host.

### Release and recovery

The extension release manifest starts at the existing package version `0.1.2`, with the bootstrap SHA set to `11ffb9d8f627a6f42d04a4aefa83c1cb92908c79`. Future extension `feat`/`fix` changes after that baseline open or refresh its Release PR. No manual bootstrap tag or desktop version edit is needed.

Marking an extension Release PR ready and merging it publishes the GitHub release and runs the workflow automatically. The GitHub release appears before Chrome submission, so it does not indicate store review approval. For failures, inspect the Chrome dashboard before rerunning the failed job. A rerun rebuilds the ZIP from the same release commit. Standard WXT submission does not automatically cancel pending reviews or skip already-submitted versions; finish those cases in the dashboard. If Google processes an upload asynchronously, wait and submit the uploaded package there rather than repeatedly uploading.

### Validation

The existing CI and Windows workflow exercise the shared setup action. Existing release-workflow tests reference the renamed app workflow. No new test scaffolding or local token commands were added. Authenticated store submission remains untested until the maintainer configures credentials.

author: tzonelb
body:
## Objective

Continue the channel-catalogue rebuild: turn Google Chat from a "coming soon" card into a genuinely working integration, the same way Slack (#13), Discord (#14), website live chat (#15), email (#16), Viber (#17), LINE (#18) and SMS (#19) were.

## Base

- Branch: `claude/platform-comprehensive-audit-ff7985`
- Base commit: `main` (includes #13–#19)

## Scope

### Included

- A company connects its own Google Chat "Chat app" (a bot scoped to its own Google Cloud project) by pasting the whole service account JSON key file Google Cloud downloads for them — there is no shorter credential a Chat app authenticates with.
- The routing identifier (`client_email`) is read out of that pasted file rather than typed — the same derived-routing shape Viber's and LINE's own provider lookups have. A Chat app has no "who am I" endpoint to ask, so the credential is instead proven genuine by using it to mint a real access token from Google's own OAuth endpoint (the standard JWT-bearer / RFC 7523 service-account flow) before the account is ever saved.
- Only the private key is sealed; the routing id and everything else in the pasted file is written unsealed, and the whole document is never stored as a unit — `google_chat_parse_service_account` narrows it down before anything is written.
- Inbound deliveries are authenticated with a Google-signed OIDC id token in `Authorization: Bearer …` — not a secret this platform and Google share, the way every other channel's signature is. Verified against Google's own public keys (`https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs`), checking signature, audience (this account's own URL, built from `config.APP_PUBLIC_URL`, the same defensive reasoning Twilio's signing URL uses against a scheme-rewriting proxy), issuer, and the fixed `chat@system.gserviceaccount.com` identity every genuine Chat delivery carries — narrowing "any Google-issued token" down to "Google Chat's own outbound calls" specifically.
- There is no `register_google_chat_webhook`: Google Chat exposes no REST endpoint for pointing a Chat app's HTTP endpoint anywhere, unlike Viber/LINE/Twilio. The operator is shown the URL after connecting and pastes it into Google Cloud Console's Chat API configuration themselves — one manual step, the same one Slack's own Event Subscriptions Request URL already asks for.
- A service account key cannot be swapped in through the update endpoint: `update_account` never routes through the JSON-parsing step a create does, so a fresh `access_token` there would be sealed exactly as pasted (the whole document, not just the key) while `external_account_id` kept naming whichever bot the *previous* key belonged to. The route refuses this outright with a clear message; rotating the key is a disconnect and reconnect, the same as email's mailbox address and SMS's Account SID/number.
- Wired into the shared outbound dispatcher in the same commit as the `SUPPORTED_CHANNELS` addition, per the established discipline.
- New dependency: `PyJWT`, added deliberately rather than hand-rolling JWK-to-RSA-key reconstruction — `cryptography` (already a dependency) does the actual RSA work underneath it.

### Not included

- Attachments/media (matches every channel here so far) and interactive buttons (appended as plain text, the same fallback Slack/Viber/LINE/SMS's senders use) — Chat's richer Cards feature is a bigger surface than this pattern has built for any one channel first.
- Anonymous "customer texts in" messaging: Google Chat has no such concept at all — every participant needs a Google identity, a Workspace member or an invited guest. This is the same shape Slack and Discord already have here (a bot DMed by whoever can reach it), not a new limitation, which is also why it sits in the "Team & collaboration" catalogue category alongside them rather than "Messaging."

## Files changed

- `backend/services/channel_account_service.py`, `backend/api/routes/channels.py`, `database/manager.py` (routing map)
- `channels/google_chat/webhook.py`, `channels/google_chat/sender.py` (new), `channels/sender.py`
- `main.py` (router registration), `requirements.txt` (PyJWT)
- `core/intent_transition.py`, `backend/api/schemas/ai_teaching.py`, `frontend/src/utils/channels.js` (channel-list parity)
- `frontend/src/pages/channels/channelCatalog.js`, `ChannelsPage.jsx`
- `tests/test_google_chat_channel.py` (new), `tests/test_a_channel_routes_only_on_its_guarded_id.py`, `tests/test_connecting_a_channel_through_the_api.py`

## Database / migration impact

- [x] None

No schema change — Google Chat reuses the existing `external_account_id`/`access_token_sealed`/`config_json` columns, the same generic slots SMS and email already use for their own credentials and non-secret settings.

## Security

- [x] No secrets/runtime/customer files added
- [x] Tenant isolation reviewed
- [x] Authorization enforced on backend

New shadow-attack regression test (`test_google_chat_delivery_reaches_its_real_owner_not_a_page_id_shadow`) confirms an attacker cannot smuggle a victim's `client_email` into the unguarded `page_id` column to hijack routing, the same class of bug already pinned for every other channel here. A dedicated HTTP-level test (`test_a_google_chat_credential_cannot_be_swapped_through_a_rename`) confirms the update endpoint refuses a credential swap while still allowing an unrelated edit through. Connect/disconnect still require the existing elevated-verification gate.

## Automated verification

- [x] Python compile (`python3 -c "import main"`)
- [x] Backend startup/fresh DB
- [x] Unit/integration/API tests
- [x] Frontend production build

Evidence/log summary: `tests/test_google_chat_channel.py` (real RS256 JWTs signed and verified with a throwaway RSA key — right/expired/wrong-audience/wrong-key/wrong-issuer/wrong-email-claim signatures, credential parsing and Google-token-mint verification, disabled/unknown-account refusal, event parsing, dispatcher wiring, token-minting sender). Full suite: **2036 passed** after merging latest `main` (the same squash-merge commit-hash divergence as the SMS round — content confirmed identical via diff before merging). `npx eslint` and `npx vite build` clean (pre-existing unrelated warnings only).

## Manual QA

Not performed against a real Google Cloud project or Chat app — no real service account key available in this environment. Connect-flow, the full inbound JWT-verification pipeline, and outbound token-minting verified with a throwaway RSA keypair and mocked Google endpoints in the test suite instead (see above).

## Protected behavior

- [x] Messenger webhook/parser/processor/sender/gateway unchanged

## Rollback plan

Revert this PR's merge commit. No schema change to reverse.

## Owner acceptance

- [ ] Explicitly accepted after QA

author: suratt0
body:
Nine commits across four pieces of work. Each is independently reviewable and
the product is working at every one of them.

## Attachments — the file picker could not be opened on a phone

All three attachment surfaces did the same thing: a `<button>` calling `.click()`
on an `<input type="file" class="hidden">`. On a desktop that works, which is why
every test passed. **On iOS Safari a `display: none` file input ignores a
programmatic click** — the picker never opened, and the camera was the only way
to attach anything. That is how it was reported: "there's only take a photo".

`FileInput` fixes the mechanism once: the input stays in the layout (`sr-only`)
and lives inside a `<label>`, so activation is native and there is no `.click()`
left to ignore. Three smaller things fell out — the ticket-level panel was
missing `multiple`, there is now a camera shortcut where the pointer is coarse,
and an image gets a thumbnail instead of a document icon.

`accept` is untouched: it names what the server takes, and `image/*` is
deliberately absent because it lets a picker offer HEIC the API then refuses.

## Tickets — "Other (please describe)"

A seventh category that asks what the problem actually is. The typed text lives
on the **ticket**, never becoming a category row: left to create rows, "เน็ตช้า"
and "เน็ทช้า" are two categories meaning one thing and every report grouping by
category quietly splits in half.

The rule is enforced in `ticketRepository.create` rather than the service,
because that repository method is the one writer the web form, the CSV import
and the inbound-mail intake all pass through. A check in the service would have
covered the form and left the other two filing "Other" with nothing written
down. Neither import nor intake is modified; they pass through the same door.

A super-admin screen lists what people typed, grouped case- and
space-insensitively, and promotes a recurring one into a real category. It
deliberately does **not** re-file the old tickets: their category is what the
desk actually worked them under.

## Settings, and permissions that a super admin can edit

The availability switch is offered only to people who can be handed a ticket — a
requester's flag is never read by routing, so for them it was a lever connected
to nothing. Hidden, not removed: the column, the routing that reads it and the
admin's own toggle are untouched.

`ROLE_PERMISSIONS` moved from a constant into `role_permissions`, and **the gate
stopped reading the access token**. A token lives fifteen minutes and cannot be
edited afterwards, so gating on it would keep a revoked permission for a quarter
of an hour — exactly the window an administrator revoking something is closing.
`requireAuth` now replaces the principal's permissions with the live ones, so
every downstream check sees the current answer. If the table is unreachable the
request is refused rather than falling back to the claim.

`super_admin`'s `*` is expanded into an explicit list, because a wildcard cannot
be un-ticked on a matrix. The cost is stated in three places: a permission added
later does not reach the top role on its own, and a test goes red until somebody
decides who gets it.

Three rules keep the desk recoverable, all server-side: `user:write` and
`permission:write` cannot leave the top role, nobody may narrow the role they
are signed in as, and every change is audited with both sides — not just the
delta.

## Customers and projects on one screen

They were two pages and the split never matched the data: a project belongs to
exactly one customer and cannot exist without one. Master–detail, with the
selection in the URL so a customer can be linked to and reloaded onto — which is
also what makes the phone layout two screens and a back button rather than two
columns squeezed into 375px.

Adding a project no longer asks which customer; it comes from the screen the
button was pressed on. A duplicate name names the project rather than the
constraint that caught it. Archiving a project now asks about open tickets as
well as members — the old guard's reasoning ("a ticket carries no project")
expired when `tickets.project_id` was added.

`/customers` redirects rather than 404s. `/projects` is kept for an admin who may
read the routing table but not change it.

## What the tests caught

Worth naming, because none was visible by reading any single file:

- `customer:write` was granted to the top role alone, silently demoting every
  admin who could previously create a customer — a demotion dressed as a
  refactor.
- The script generating the permission migration mis-parsed a single-line array
  and dropped `ticket:create` from `user`. A test now reads the migration SQL and
  compares it against the constant.
- The pending-attachment thumbnail cleared its own object URL in an effect
  cleanup, which under StrictMode raced the second effect and left no image.
- Every labelled button on the new screen was 36px tall, under the 44px a
  fingertip needs.

## Verification

```
backend  tsc + lint          clean
backend  unit                349 passed (28 files)
backend  integration         569 passed (20 files)
frontend tsc + lint          clean
frontend unit                227 passed (26 files)
frontend e2e                 admin-customers 16, mobile 4, category-other 5,
                             attach-picker 5, settings-availability 4,
                             plus the existing ticket/permission suites
```

## Notes for the reviewer

- Branched from `origin/main`. The error-code work on `fix/auth-copy-language`
  is separate and still open; when both land, `CATEGORY_DETAIL_REQUIRED`,
  `PROJECT_HAS_OPEN_TICKETS` and `PROJECT_NAME_TAKEN` need adding to
  `ERROR_CODES` and the dictionary, or they fall back to the generic sentence.
- The permission cache is per process. A deployment running several API
  instances should move it to a shared cache or drop it; nothing outside
  `permission.repository.ts` reads the table.

author: lihi-ai
body:
Part of #518 (rally 2, point 2 — frozen in the issue comment of 2026-09-14). Class S; one mechanism: the two remaining Toolbox drawers get their own placement+clip.

## Mechanism
`renderDirty` keeps a whole-window fallback under any viewport because two replay paths cannot draw under a partial projection clip: `ToolboxCellContext::draw` painted its unclipped `rect_` with no clip of its own, and `redrawPopupHit` painted the popup face from the hit ledger's *clipped* `hit.rect` as if it were the outline (frame, arrow and label shift for a partially clipped popup). Text, EditText and RectSurface already draw their geometry from `rect_` under `ToolboxPaintClip(paintRect_)` captured at projection.

## Change
- Cell and PopupMenu capture `paintRect_` in their layout/updateRect through `intersectWithProjectionClip`, same writer and moment as `rect_`, cleared on detach; they draw from `rect_` under `ToolboxPaintClip(paintRect_)`.
- The popup face is painted by one private context function used by `draw()` (full render, no erase — the window was erased) and the new `repaint()` (erases `paintRect_` first). The 1 px gray shadow at `rect_.right/bottom` lies inside the clip rect (clip widened by 1 px; geometry unchanged).
- The controller's popup replay calls `hit.context->repaint()`; the ledger keeps only what hit-testing, dirty intersection and enabled-state reconciliation read (`rect`, `context`, `enabled`); items/selectedIndex/onChange/lineHeight/menuId/boundary copies are gone.
- Cell label ink that overflowed `rect_` is now clipped (intended: the other rails never painted it). No control item, no controller clip, viewport gates untouched (PR c-2).

## Pins (standalone `LokaPaintDamage68K`, red on `main`, green after)
- `cell-replay-clipped`: a Cell straddling a viewport bottom; after a dirty replay covering its full rect, ink below the viewport is white, inside is black.
- `popup-replay-geometry`: a popup partially clipped on the right; the frame/label row after replay equals the row after full render, nothing painted right of the viewport edge.
- `cell-ink-clipped-to-rect`: a Cell narrower than its centered label; label ink outside `rect_` is white.
- 24 scenario cells expected unchanged (MineSweeper's one-character labels fit their 24 px cells).

## Evidence (host, candidate 5daa04a8)
| Check | Result |

author: jnzader
body:
The local GitHub parity mode now separates what was actually reproduced locally from what remains a non-local follow-up. Previously, successful local commands and unavailable GitHub-only work were all surfaced with generic PASS/SKIP wording, which made the report easier to misread as complete workflow certification.

This PR labels the parity report by evidence class:
- LOCAL RUN / LOCAL PASS for commands and tools reproduced on the developer machine.
- FOLLOW-UP (LOCAL TOOL MISSING) when a GitHub CI tool such as ruff or bwrap is absent locally.
- FOLLOW-UP (GITHUB-HOSTED) for the Linux/Windows hook runtime matrix.
- FOLLOW-UP (GLOBAL SIDE EFFECT) for the packed-tarball global-install self-CI path.

The --github-parity --json refusal now uses the same LOCAL/FOLLOW-UP terminology, and the commands docs document the evidence split.

Evidence:
- pnpm exec vitest run src/commands/ci.test.ts -t "GitHub Actions parity" passed: 2 tests, 148 skipped.
- pnpm exec vitest run src/cli/dispatch/ci-json-run.test.ts passed: 5 tests.

- Commit and push hooks ran lint plus build and passed.

## What and why

`DocumentArtifactTests` (#155) proves the document pipeline end to end — posting requests an artefact, the worker
renders and stores it, the stored checksum equals the bytes. **It never compares a printed figure with a stored
figure**, so a renderer handed the wrong model, or printing a column it had mislabelled, would pass every test in
the suite. That is the parent's outstanding acceptance criterion — *"PDF totals and tax components match the
persisted calculation snapshot"* — and this slice closes it.

`PdfSnapshotAgreementTests` reads the bytes back out of the object store through `OpenInvoiceAsync`, extracts the
page's own text layer, and compares every figure with the snapshot read through `IPricingService.FindSnapshotAsync`
— **the published contract, not the table, and not the `DocumentModel` the renderer was handed** (which would only
prove the renderer agrees with itself). Two scenes, because one cannot catch a place-of-supply regression:
intra-state must print CGST and SGST and no IGST, inter-state the reverse.

It also writes the accountant's sample pack and the review record that puts the presentation questions to them.
**#42 stays open until the accountant signs.**

## Linked issue

Refs #326 (E09-F02-10, a sub-issue of the Billing invoicing parent)

## How it was verified

- [x] **Integration tier**, full, run 1: **676 of 678 passed**. The two failures are not this change's — see Evidence

author: platocres
body:
## What & why

Builds the top of the documented next-build queue (`docs/NEXT_BUILD.md` #1 / `docs/ROADMAP.md` §5): **playbooks**. The last several PRs (#7–#13) drove parser coverage deep; this converts that maturity into operator leverage — gather a batch of related evidence in one deliberate, ordered move.

A playbook is a **named, ordered sequence of pack actions, stored as data** (`obol/playbooks/*.json`). Each step references an existing pack action by id. Running a step goes through the **exact same** command templating, scope enforcement, runner (`runner.run_command`), parser (`parsers.parse_action_output`), and `.obol` store as `obol run` — there is one shared execution path (`cli._run_action`), **no second runner and no second state store** (AGENTS.md #3/#4).

## What's included

- **`obol/playbook.py`** — `Playbook`/`PlaybookStep` model, `list_playbooks()`, `load_playbook()`, and `resolve_step[s]()` that map each step to a real pack `Action`. Pure data/model, no execution.
- **`obol/playbooks/ad-recon.json`** — first playbook: nmap quick scan → targeted `-sC -sV` → DC identify → anonymous LDAP → SMB/RID user enum. The RID-brute step is `require_approval`. Plus `obol/playbooks/NOTICE.md` keeping the GPL pack-attribution boundary intact (playbooks reference action ids; they don't fold in pack content).
- **CLI**:
  - `obol playbooks` — list playbooks.
  - `obol playbook <name>` — render the exact command plan; **executes nothing**.
  - `obol playbook <name> --step N` — run one step through the shared runner/parser; `--dry-run` previews just that step.
  - `require_approval` steps refuse to run without `--approve` (noisy/risky gating), modeled on Pentest Companion's per-step approval.
- **`board.render_playbook`** — plan view (rich + plain fallback), staying within the product's UX guardrails: an ordered plan with exact commands and an `(--approve)` marker; no proves/blocked language.
- **Ledger** records `playbook`/`playbook_step` lineage per run (flows into `obol report`).
- **`cmd_run` refactor** — extracted the run→parse→record body into `_run_action`; behavior-preserving (`command_index + 1 == args.cmd`).

## Design choices

- Bare `obol playbook <name>` is always a safe plan view — execution requires an explicit `--step`, so nothing runs by surprise.
- Later steps whose tokens aren't filled yet (e.g. `{{nmap_ports}}` before the scan) keep the token visible in the plan; the runner then refuses the unfilled token — honest gating rather than a fake "blocked" panel.
- A full-sequence `--run-all` was deliberately left out of this first slice to keep execution one deliberate step at a time (noted as a follow-up in `docs/NEXT_BUILD.md`).

## Tests

New `tests/test_playbook.py` locks in: every step resolves to a real pack action (drift guard against pack renames), approval gating on the noisy step, and scoped/templated command rendering. **58 tests pass** locally under CI's warning-as-error flags, on both the rich and plain render paths. Verified end-to-end against a faked `nmap`: a step executes, parses evidence into narrow facts, and writes the playbook lineage to the ledger.

author: emeraldcoastsystemsgroup
body:
The mirror of #401, found in three consecutive **real alerts** rather than in a fixture.

#401 stopped a skipped gate being reported as FIXED. It did not stop the same skip corrupting the other direction. When a run fails early it appends skip markers and every downstream gate silently *leaves* its failing set — so the next run diffs against a baseline that never measured them, and every long-standing failure reads as brand new.

**What actually went out on 2026-09-13 (night 50):**

> `NEW: store-compatibility unit lint security-policy e2e-green trivy`

Only `security-policy` was new. `unit`, `lint`, `e2e-green` and `trivy` had been red since **July** — they were absent from night 49 only because it died at `head-src` and skipped the node gates. Night 48 was the same. A false NEW is worse than the flat wording BUG-22 replaced: a gate that cries NEW every other night trains you to ignore the word, which is the exact failure this whole line of work exists to remove.

**Same log, fixed code:**

> `NEW: security-policy (night 50)`
> `… Compared against 2026-09-11T01:05:34 — the last run that measured every gate; 1 intervening run skipped gates and cannot say what is new.`

## The rule

The baseline is the most recent prior run that **skipped nothing** — usually, but not always, the immediately preceding run. A green run qualifies (it measured everything and nothing failed). When no such run exists there is no honest baseline and nothing is claimed new. When intervening runs were stepped over, the body names the baseline so the NEW/already-known split stays auditable from the alert alone.

## Guards — 18 → 23

Key case is built from the verbatim nights 48–50 log lines. Also: the baseline is named when runs were stepped over, a green run is a valid baseline, and nothing is new when every prior run skipped.

One existing case changed: the de-duplication fixture carried `trivy-skipped` in its *baseline*, so it was accidentally exercising baseline selection instead of de-duplication. Its markers are now ordinary gate names and it asserts the same thing it always meant to.

## Documentation

`docs/runbooks/local-ci.md` gains two sections:

- **Reading the failure alert** — every subject shape and what it means, the three rules behind the wording and the false alert each one prevents.
- **BUG-22 — what is done, and how to continue** — the two gates fixed, the five open items with a suggested order, and why a red night is not yet evidence about the code.

Plus four operational hazards that each cost a night: editing `ci-local.sh` while a run holds the lock (bash reads by byte offset), the unbounded `rm -rf` in `prepare_head_src` that wedged for 9 hours, `gitleaks` exiting 0 with unread files, and MSYS `tar` reading a Windows path as a remote host to produce a silently empty export.

## Validation

`23/23` · `tsc --noEmit` clean · `bash -n` clean · LF endings · the real log re-summarized end to end.

Committed via the private-index recipe — HEAD is on another session's branch with their WIP in the tree; nothing of theirs was read or written. Exactly 3 files.

| "`GET /api/agents` returns bare strings today, so neither the UI nor `mercuryctl` can know what a server accepts" | The handler returns `agents`, `defaultAgent` **and** `capabilities` — and **the comment above it cites §13.6 as its own spec**. The code points at a document describing the state before the code landed. |
| "`mercuryctl agents list` **gains** a goal column" | Already renders `AGENT \| GOALS \| SKILLS \|`, three-state `goalsCell`, absent capability = `unknown` not `no` |
| "The UI disables the goal fields with the reason attached…" | **Genuinely unbuilt** — `ui/index.js` has *zero* `capabilities` references; create form has no goal field |

Only the third is real work, and that stays open as #575 — including the product question of whether the dashboard should set goals at all. **This PR does not answer #575.**

## Why it is separate from #575

§13.6 is what someone implements *from*, and §13.7 says it in its own words: *"a stale table is worse than none because it looks authoritative."* A person picking up **either** answer to #575 would have started by adding an API field and a CLI column that both already exist.

## Guard — 6 mutations, all firing

`test/goalSurface.test.ts` gains two tests that bind the section to the **code** rather than to prose:

- reintroduce "returns bare strings today" → fires
- reintroduce "gains a goal column" → fires
- drop the "Not built" marker → fires
- drop the #575 link → fires
- **make `ui/index.js` read `capabilities` → fires** — the "not built" claim is checked against the UI, so the day someone resolves #575 the section fails and says so
- **stop returning `capabilities` from the endpoint → fires** — the shipped claim is checked against the handler

The last two are the point. A doc assertion that only reads other docs drifts exactly the way this section just did.

## Verified, not assumed

Removing `docs/goals.md` from the `contract_docs` path allowlist makes `ciWorkflow.test.ts` fail with *"read but never triggered: docs/goals.md"* — proving the new read is visible to the CI guard. The previous change to this suite nearly shipped a test the guard could not see at all.

## Measured

`goalSurface.test.ts` 14/14, `ciWorkflow.test.ts` 4/4. Full suite green: **1105 core (+2)** + 202 fleet + 117 Atlas + 278 client, exit 0. Typecheck clean.

## What
Adds a thread-affine peer-release funnel diagnostic to track the lifetime relationship between a native `DependencyObject` and its managed peer, verifying that peer release happens on the correct (owning) thread.

## Why
XAML objects exist as a native/managed pair whose lifetimes must stay in sync, and the peer must be released on its owning thread. This diagnostic funnels peer release through a single checked point, gated behind a runtime-enabled feature, so cross-thread or out-of-order releases are caught early.

## Changes
- Route peer release through a thread-affine funnel diagnostic (`WeakReferenceSourceNoThreadId.cpp`, `depends.cpp`).
- Add a runtime-enabled feature flag to gate the diagnostic (`RuntimeFeatureData.cpp`, `RuntimeEnabledFeaturesEnum.h`).
- Add lifetime unit tests and scaffolding covering the funnel (`LifetimeUnitTests.*`, `FakeDXamlCore.h`).

Net (this PR's own commit): **7 files changed, 143 insertions, 1 deletion**.

## Dependency / stacking
This change consumes `GetPeerLifetimeState`, `TransitionPeerState`, and the `PeerLifetimeState` enum (`Releasing`/`TornDown`), which are introduced by the peer-lifetime-state work in **#11875**. It is therefore **stacked on `#11875`** (base branch `user/protikbiswas/pillar-a-peer-lifetime`) rather than duplicating that commit here — duplicating it would collide when both PRs merge. Once **#11875** merges into `main`, GitHub will automatically retarget this PR to `main`.

Not dependent on #11876 (the tracked-storage codegen PR); that PR does not define these symbols.

author: syntaxwanderer
body:
## Summary

A deferred slot is rendered **twice** — by Twig on the server and by `semitexa-twig.js` on the client — and the client subset has no functions, no filters beyond `|raw` and no ternary. Anything outside it renders as an **empty string with no error**, so the divergence is invisible until someone notices missing text.

## Changes

The check runs where the framework says *"the client can render this"*: at publish. Both publish paths call it — `initialize()` sweeps every deferred slot at boot, `publishSlot()` covers whatever that missed behind `ensurePublishedPath()`'s cache.

**Not the render path.** Publishing happens once per slot; validating per render would pay an AST walk per request for an answer that cannot change between them.

**Not a new gate either.** `ai:verify` already runs `lint:deferred-twig` when a template changes — `VerificationPlanner` has carried it since it was wired, which I checked rather than assumed. Anyone working in this workspace is covered. What is not covered is a consumer project editing its own template and never running the linter, which is exactly who `publishSlot()` serves.

**Dev throws, production does not.** A developer wants to be stopped where it is cheap; an end user should not get a 500 for a template that merely degrades, and a template already in production has already shipped. Production logs the same detail at the same moment.

Detection and decision are separate methods because they differ in testability: detection needs a booted module registry, the decision does not.

## Checks

- `composer phpstan` — 177, unchanged
- `bin/semitexa test:run` — 8416 PHPUnit + 97 E2E green
- `bin/semitexa lint:deferred-twig` — all templates compatible

## What to review

**The second commit exists because the first one put the check in the wrong method.** The edit matched `$content = file_get_contents($templatePath);` as a *substring*, and the first occurrence sits one indent level deeper inside `initialize()`'s loop — so it spliced into that loop with broken indentation while `publishSlot()`, which the commit message described, got nothing. It was syntactically valid, the suite stayed green, and the unit tests drove the private methods directly, so nothing said a word. Worth reading the two commits together rather than only the result.

## What to verify

Four deterministic tests cover the decision; detection stays covered by `DeferredTemplateCompatibilityValidatorTest`'s nine. A test asserting `APP_ENV` defaults to `prod` is **documented rather than written** — `Environment` reads the workspace `.env`, which declares `dev`, so `putenv()` cannot produce the unset case.

author: bendourthe
body:
Two behaviours the harness was missing. They share one script because both parse the same thing: a plan's phase headings, checkboxes, and per-phase routing fields.

## 1. Progress at every phase boundary

`python scripts/plan_status.py --plan <file>` prints where a multi-session plan actually stands, so a reader does not have to open it:

```
**Plan**: Plan - Document and Deck Quality Gates
**Target version**: v4.11.2

| Phase | Status | Tasks |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Geometric audit foundation | complete | 3/3 |
| 2. Type roles and the SVG render ratio | complete | 3/3 |
...
| 7. Architecture Refactor, Known-Gaps Reconciliation, and CI/CD | in progress | 0/7 |

**6 of 7 phases complete; 21 of 28 tasks.**
```

Wired into `implement-phase`. It is **derived, never hand-written** — a hand-written table is a second source of truth that drifts on the first missed tick.

## 2. Next-plan handoff after a release

`python scripts/plan_status.py --next` closes a release with the command for the next session:

```
**Next plan**: Plan - Cache accounting and diagram quality
**Target version**: v4.11.1
**Open**: 25 of 25 tasks across 6 phases

/implement v4.11.1 in-full

**Use frontier tier at max effort for the whole run.**

| Platform | Model | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| Anthropic | `claude-fable-5-1` | max |
| OpenAI | `gpt-6-astra` | max |
| Google | `gemini-3.8-flash` | max |
| Cursor | `cursor-grok-4.6` | max |
```

Wired into `/update release`.

**One recommendation, and it is the MAXIMUM rather than the average.** `in-full` executes every phase in a single invocation, so the setting must carry the hardest phase. A phase-by-phase breakdown would be correct advice for a command nobody is running, and the modal value would under-provision the phase most likely to need the headroom.

Per-platform ids come from the plan's own dated `## Current model map`. The script **never invents a model id** — an absent or stale map is reported as such, because a confidently wrong id is worse than none. Cursor, OpenCode and Copilot have no scriptable switch, so the handoff says to set those in the picker.

## The selector was wrong first, and the fix is the interesting part

The first version proposed **v3.0.0 while the repository sat at v4.11.0**.

Plans from shipped cycles keep unticked boxes forever — some predate the checkbox convention, others were closed without anyone ticking them. An unfiltered scan returns archaeology rather than a queue. It now floors on the released version from `plugin.json`, and `test_a_shipped_cycle_is_not_proposed_as_next` asserts it.

That fix surfaced real data debt: **v4.11.0's `T031` (publication and integration) was never ticked** even though the release shipped on 2026-09-13. Corrected here; the plan is marked released at 31/31.

## Notes for review

- Registered in **both** installers, per the rule that a `scripts/*.py` file is copied by explicit name rather than by folder.
- 9 tests, including the maximum-not-average rule, the version floor, the no-invented-id rule, and a parse of this repository's real plans rather than fixtures only.
- Fast profile 14/14.
- Deliberately **not** folded into v4.11.2: that plan is about document quality and its final phase exists to verify exactly this kind of scope boundary.

## How to test

```bash
python scripts/plan_status.py --plan docs/releases/v4/v4.11/plans/v4.11.0-interactive-handbooks-and-presentation-default.md
python scripts/plan_status.py --next
python -m pytest tests/validators/test_plan_status.py -q
```

author: antsf
body:
## Summary

Applies the generic CI/release-automation patterns to this Next.js repo.

**Tech stack:** Next.js 16 (App Router) + TypeScript + Vitest, deployed via Vercel.

### Pattern 1 — concurrency cancel-in-progress
Added to `ci.yml` and the new `release.yml`. Superseded runs on rapid pushes get cancelled instead of queuing.

### Pattern 2 — coverage gate
Real Vitest tests are already wired into CI (66 tests across 5 files). Added `@vitest/coverage-v8`, enabled `lcov` + `text` reporters in `vitest.config.ts`, and measured the actual baseline locally:

```
Line coverage: 65.10% (97/149)
```

Gate set to **60%** (a few points below baseline) via `VeryGoodOpenSource/very_good_coverage@v3`, acting as an anti-regression floor rather than a blocker.

### Pattern 3 — tag-triggered release
`CHANGELOG.md` uses parseable `## [X.Y.Z] — date` headers, so added `release.yml`:
- `verify` job: typecheck, test, build, and confirms the pushed tag matches `package.json`'s version.
- `release` job: extracts the matching CHANGELOG section and publishes a GitHub Release via `softprops/action-gh-release@v2`.

### Pattern 4 — publish step commented out
Vercel's own GitHub integration already auto-deploys on push/tag, so there's no separate publish step to enable today. Added a commented-out `deploy` job placeholder in `release.yml` with a note that any manual deploy trigger needs explicit go-ahead before being uncommented.

### Other changes
- `package-lock.json` updated for the new `@vitest/coverage-v8` devDependency.
- `.gitignore`: added `coverage/` (generated output, shouldn't be tracked).

No behavior change to the app itself — CI/CD config only.

author: charlessmart
body:
Stacked on #55. Completes step 4 of the refactor plan.

## Problem

Tailwind and vanilla-extract interpretation lived in `packages/plugin`, which is a **build-tool host**. The browser runtime cannot depend on a build-tool host, so when the inspector needed to read a Tailwind v4 alpha utility it could not reuse the grammar and reimplemented it:

```
packages/plugin/src/adapters/tailwindV4.ts     /^bg-([\w-]+)\/(\d{1,3}%?)$/
packages/inspector/src/tokens/resolution.ts    /^bg-([\w-]+)\/(\d{1,3}%?)$/
```

Byte-identical, and free to drift. These two are not merely similar code: the build side decides *which token* a utility refers to, and the runtime side attributes a user's colour edit to that token. If they ever disagreed about an edge case, an edit would be written against the wrong token.

The location was the cause, so the fix is a location.

## Change

Interpretation moves to `@nudge-ui/css/dialects` — a package **both** the plugin and the inspector already depend on, with no runtime imports at all, so it is reachable from the browser bundle.

The entry point is one pure function:

```ts
interpretDialects(evidence: DialectEvidence): DialectInterpretation
```

A host supplies the evidence it can actually observe, and gets back the inventory contributions that evidence supports. Hosts keep what is genuinely theirs — loading a module, resolving a config, watching a transform pipeline.

Purity is the point, not a side effect. It means dialect behaviour is tested directly, with no build tool standing up, and that **any two hosts supplying the same evidence provably get the same tokens**. There is a test asserting exactly that.

## Honest capability reporting

Hosts differ enormously in what they can see, and the plan asked not to paper over it. `interpretDialects` reports what each dialect was proven by:

```ts
[
  { dialect: "tailwind-v3",    evidence: "config",   tokenCount: 12 },
  { dialect: "tailwind-v4",    evidence: "css",      tokenCount: 0  },
  { dialect: "vanilla-extract", evidence: "none",    tokenCount: 0  },
]
```

A host that can only scan `.css` off disk now has something to say about *why* its catalog is thin, instead of serving a quietly smaller one that looks complete.

## Deletions

- `TokenAdapter.resolveClassName`, `TokenMapping`, and the registry that dispatched to them. Nothing outside their own tests ever called them; runtime class resolution happens in the inspector by a different route.
- `mergeVanillaExtractContract` and `tailwindV3ColorDeclaration` — unreachable. I initially carried both into the new module before checking, and removed them once I confirmed nothing reaches them.
- 16 lines of dialect internals re-exported from the plugin's public API.
- A `./vanilla-extract-runtime` subpath export pointing at a deleted file.

## A defect this surfaced

`verify-packages` caught that #55 left `@nudge-ui/standalone` exporting `./html/identity` after the module moved — a subpath pointing at a file that is no longer built. That check is not on the default CI path, so it went unnoticed. **Fixed on the #55 branch** rather than here, so that PR is correct on its own, then merged forward. All 11 packages now verify.

## Net

-133 source lines here. Cumulatively across #52–#56 the source tree is +66 lines, which I want to be straight about: the consolidation so far has bought structure and deleted duplication, but the large removals land in step 6 when the old host packages go.

## Verification

`build:packages`, `typecheck`, `lint`, `test:unit` (1253 inspector tests, 68 plugin tests, 31 new dialect tests), `check:boundaries`, and `verify-packages` all pass. The plugin's "publishes the inventory snapshot verbatim" test compares generation hashes against a hand-built inventory, so a change in the facts these contributions produce would fail it.

Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com)

author: tmayad
body:
## Thinking Path

> - Paperclip is the open source app people use to manage AI agents for work
> - Agents run on provider adapters, and many operators run them on a Claude or Codex subscription instead of a metered API key
> - Paperclip budgets are built on `cost_events`. Subscription runs record 0 cents, so a money budget can never limit subscription usage
> - Paperclip already reads the provider's subscription windows (session and week, percent used and reset time) for the Costs page, but nothing enforces them
> - A money-style hard stop would be the wrong tool: a subscription window resets on its own, so pausing the scope and asking the Board to "raise the budget" is noise that also needs a human to undo
> - This pull request adds `subscription_percent` budget policies on provider windows and enforces them by deferring queued runs to the window reset, with no incident, pause, or board escalation
> - The benefit is that operators can keep headroom in their subscription windows for interactive use, or stop low-priority agents from burning the weekly window, and work resumes on its own

## Linked Issues or Issue Description

Related issues (none is closed by this change; each note says what this PR does and does not cover):

- Refs #8856 — proposes budget metrics for subscription billing, including a `quota_window_pct` hard-stop that reserves headroom for interactive use. This PR implements that metric as `subscription_percent` (defer to the window reset rather than a hard-stop); the `tokens` and `runs` metrics proposed there are not included.
- Refs #5521 — Anthropic usage-limit aware company pause plus scheduled resume. Same motivation; this PR reaches the outcome without a pause flag by deferring each claim to the provider's reported reset, using the shared quota snapshot instead of per-run failures.
- Refs #3406 — subscription-aware budget management for Claude Max plans. Covers the "budgets are fictional under a flat-rate plan" part; the usage-triggered review loop is out of scope.
- Refs #11597 — the stored `provider_quota` reset time never gates new run creation. With a `subscription_percent` policy at 100%, the gate now defers claims while the provider window is saturated; gating on the reset time recorded by a failed run itself is still not done here.
- Refs #1756 and #339 — token budgets and estimated cost for subscription-billed agents. Complementary metrics for the same gap; not addressed by this change.

Feature request fields:

**Problem / motivation**

Operators on a Claude or Codex subscription cannot express "do not start new agent runs while my session window is above 80% used" or "leave 10% of the weekly window for me". `billed_cents` budgets never move for subscription runs because their cost events are recorded at 0 cents. The provider quota windows are shown on the Costs page but are purely informational.

**Proposed solution**

- Add the `subscription_percent` metric and the `provider_session` / `provider_week` window kinds to `budget_policies`. `amount` is a whole percent of the provider window. Two policies on one scope combine as OR.
- Give every provider quota window a stable `key` (`five_hour`, `seven_day`, ...) so policies match by key instead of display label.
- Add a memoized process-wide quota snapshot reader with a TTL, so enforcement never calls the rate-limited usage endpoints per dispatch.
- Enforce the policy in `claimQueuedRun`, the last step before adapter invocation. A saturated window **defers** the run: it becomes a `scheduled_retry` at `resets_at + 30s` with reason `subscription_window_wait`, and the ordinary due-retry loop promotes it again. Timer heartbeats are skipped quietly, like the daily cap. The issue keeps its status and assignee, the wake stays queued, and no comment, incident, approval, or recovery action is written.
- The gate fails open when the quota snapshot is unavailable. The provider's real limit still applies and is handled by the existing `provider_quota` recovery.
- A run that has been waiting longer than `PAPERCLIP_SUBSCRIPTION_WINDOW_WAIT_MAX_MS` (default 8 days) since its first consecutive deferral is cancelled with `subscription_window_wait_exhausted` through the same pre-invocation path as the daily cap, because that only happens when the quota snapshot is stale or the account is wedged. Only this gate's own deferrals count toward the bound, and a reported reset later than the deadline is clamped to it.
- Show the policies on Costs → Budgets as a "Subscription usage limits" section (session and week cards for the organization scope, seeded from the live quota snapshot) and render `subscription_percent` policies in percent in `BudgetPolicyCard`.

**Alternatives considered**

- Reusing `getInvocationBlock` for the new policy. Every consumer of that block treats it as terminal: queued runs are cancelled, scheduled retries are suppressed permanently, `budget_blocked` is non-retryable in recovery, and disposition repair escalates straight to the Board. A self-resetting window would generate blocked issues and recovery actions that resolve themselves an hour later. The deferral path avoids all of that.
- Mapping subscription usage onto fake cost events so the existing money budget triggers. Costs are a monotonic monthly sum, so window resets would need negative cost events, the scope would still need a human to un-pause, and the fake cents would pollute every cost report.

**Roadmap alignment**

Extends the existing budget policy model (`doc/plans/2026-03-14-budget-policies-and-enforcement.md`) without changing the money budget behaviour. Details in `doc/plans/2026-09-13-subscription-window-budgets.md`.

## What Changed

- `packages/shared`: `BUDGET_METRICS` gains `subscription_percent`; `BUDGET_WINDOW_KINDS` gains `provider_session` and `provider_week`; new `QUOTA_WINDOW_KEYS` and `SUBSCRIPTION_BUDGET_WINDOW_QUOTA_KEYS`; `upsertBudgetPolicySchema` rejects mismatched metric/window pairs and percent limits above 100; `QuotaWindow.key` added.
- `packages/adapter-utils`: `QuotaWindow.key` added to the adapter contract (optional, backward compatible).
- `packages/adapters/claude-local`, `packages/adapters/codex-local`: quota windows carry stable keys. Per-model Codex limits keep a null key so gates never read them by mistake.
- `server/src/services/quota-windows.ts`: `createQuotaSnapshotReader` / `readQuotaSnapshot` memoize `fetchAllQuotaWindows` with a TTL (`PAPERCLIP_QUOTA_SNAPSHOT_TTL_MS`, default 60s), share one in-flight fetch, and never throw.

**Submitter note**

Model: Claude Opus
Harness: Claude Code

# Dead Counter Reset Elision in the Word Exponent Byte Tail

Parent: `16faf70a368a1f53e92f2501348caa183b2e2b21` — the public MODEXP crown for
this track. The working tree is that commit plus the single mechanism described
below; nothing else under `Challenge/Modexp/Submission` is touched.

## The fragment

The single-word path (`modulusSize input ≤ 32`) walks the exponent one byte at a
time. Each byte is consumed by an eight-step square-and-multiply sequence that
is physically unrolled only four times: the four product bodies live at pcs
2506, 2528, 2550 and 2572, and a bit counter riding in stack slot 2
distinguishes the first half of the byte (`counter = 0`) from the second half
(`counter = 4`). After the fourth body the control fragment at pc 2594 advances
the counter by four and loops back to the JUMPDEST at pc 2505 while the counter
is still below eight:

```
2594: SWAP1  PUSH1 4  ADD  SWAP1  DUP2  PUSH1 8  GT  PUSH2 2505  JUMPI
```

When the second half finishes, the counter is eight, the JUMPI falls through,
and four bytes at pc 2607 run before the tail:

```
2607: SWAP1  POP  PUSH0  SWAP1        (the parent crown: 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10 gas)
2611: POP  PUSH1 224  JUMP
```

Those four bytes exist to put the counter back to zero. The stack layout is
`[base-1, counter, byte, offset, outer, acc, base, m]`, so the fragment swaps
the counter up, pops the stale eight, pushes a fresh zero and swaps it back
down. It costs ten gas and it runs once for every exponent byte on the word
path.

## Why the reset is dead

The counter slot is never read again after pc 2606. Tracing the two consumers
settles it:

- pc 2611 (`POP`) drops `base - 1`, not the counter; the byte-loop tail is
  reached at pc 224 with the counter on top of the stack.
- pcs 225/226/227 are `POP POP POP`. The first of those three pops is exactly
  the counter slot. Only then does the loop do `PUSH1 1 / ADD` on the outer byte
  index and jump back to the byte-loop head at pc 205.
- The next byte re-enters the unrolled block through pc 212…220, and the final
  instruction before the jump is a bare `PUSH0` at pc 219. That `PUSH0` — not
  the reset fragment — is what establishes `counter = 0` for the next byte.

So the value written at pc 2607 is consumed by a `POP` four instructions later
and by nothing else. The whole fragment is dead work repeated once per exponent
byte. This submission deletes the work while keeping the four bytes, so no
instruction in the program moves.

## The mechanism

Bytes 2607…2610 become four `JUMPDEST`s:

```
2607: JUMPDEST JUMPDEST JUMPDEST JUMPDEST     (1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 gas)
2611: POP  PUSH1 224  JUMP
```

`JUMPDEST` is the cheapest one-byte opcode in the Osaka schedule (one gas) and
the only one that is both stack-neutral and fully inert, which is what a
width-preserving landing pad has to be. Execution now falls from the JUMPI
straight through to the tail, carrying the terminal counter value eight into the
slot that pc 225 pops. Four bytes in, four bytes out: the stream is still 5312
bytes and 4082 instructions, every program counter and every instruction index
downstream of 2610 is unchanged, and no jump literal anywhere in the artifact
has to be rewritten. The four new jump destinations are unreachable — nothing in
the program pushes 2607, 2608, 2609 or 2610 — so they widen the valid-destination
set without widening reachable behaviour.

## Gas effect

Ten gas become four, once per exponent byte consumed on the word path. The
scored corpus is 44 vectors; 32 of them are `generated 256-bit #NN full
exponent` cases with 32-byte exponents, and the BN254 Fermat and modular
inversion vectors are likewise single-word moduli that run this tail once per
exponent byte. That is on the order of a thousand executions of the fragment
across the corpus, so the mechanism removes roughly six thousand gas from the
measured total. The saving does not depend on the per-run corpus seed: every
single-word vector pays the tail once per exponent byte regardless of which byte
values the seed draws, and no vector pays it more or less often than before.

The accounting is visible in the proof constants. The eighth unrolled copy
`gasSteps_bitCopy7` is body (68) + control (34) + tail, so it drops from 110 to
106; the whole byte loop `gasSteps_bitLoop` from 643 to 639 (11 entry + 10 head +
69 + 68 + 68 + 102 + 69 + 68 + 68 + 106); one exponent iteration
`gasSteps_expIteration` from 725 to 721 (45 enter + 639 loop + 37 finish); and
the closed form for the exponent loop from `725 * exponentSize input` to
`721 * exponentSize input`.

## What the patch contains

Everything lives under `Challenge/Modexp/Submission`:

- `bytecode.hex` — the four bytes at offset 2607 rewritten to `5b5b5b5b`.
  Length stays 5312; the `POP` at 2611 is untouched.
- `Bytes.lean` — `submissionChunk40` (offsets 2560…2623) regenerated from the
  patched stream so the proof-bound `ByteArray` stays byte-for-byte equal to the
  hex artifact. Re-parsing all 83 chunks reproduces the 5312-byte stream exactly.
- `Proofs/Bytecode/Artifact.lean` — the four `submissionInstructions` entries at
  indices 1973…1976 become `.op .JUMPDEST`. Instruction count and
  `assemble_submissionInstructions` are unaffected because both the widths and
  the number of instructions are preserved.
- `Proofs/Bytecode/WordBitsFourCore.lean` — `resetProgram` is now four
  `JUMPDEST`s, and `run_reset` states the honest transition: from pc 2607 with
  the counter at eight to pc 2611 with the stack completely unchanged. The
  stack-depth hypothesis `h7` that the old pop/push pair needed is gone, since
  the landing pad never changes the depth. The proof is deliberately not a
  single monolithic `simp` over the four-instruction program: it is four
  one-instruction lemmas (`run_pad2607` … `run_pad2610`), each an exact copy of
  the `run_start` pattern already proved in this file for the `JUMPDEST` at pc
  2505, chained with `runInstructions_append_some` exactly the way `run_body`
  chains its select/factor/product segments. Each step is therefore discharged
  by a tactic script that is known to close this precise goal shape, and the
  composition is a plain `exact`: the concatenated program reduces definitionally
  to `resetProgram`, so no rewriting of the program list is needed.
- `Proofs/Bytecode/WordBitsFour.lean` — `reset_cost` restated at 4, with the
  `lift_cost` static-cost argument moved in lock-step. The `resetBlock` slice

- `Proofs/Bytecode/WordBitsFourCopies.lean` — `gasSteps_copy7` now lands on

- `Proofs/Bytecode/Word.lean` — `bitCounter` extended past the loop: it is 0 for

- `Proofs/Bytecode/WordLoopGuardHead.lean` — `bitFinishDispatchState` is the

body:
두 가지를 고친다.

## 1. 터미널을 우클릭 → `↗ 탐색기로 열기`

창 메뉴 **맨 아래**에 항목이 하나 붙는다. 그 터미널이 지금 서 있는 폴더(`pwd`)를 윈도우 탐색기로 연다.

어느 폴더를 열지는 Rust 가 정한다(`pane_reveal_cwd`). 아는 순서대로 물러난다.

| 순서 | 폴더 | 토스트 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 셸이 **지금** 알려 주고 있는 폴더(`live_cwd`) | `탐색기 · <경로>` |
| 2 | 창에 마지막으로 적힌 폴더 — 셸 통합이 없거나 셸이 끝났을 때 | `… 마지막으로 알던 폴더를 엽니다 · <경로>` |
| 3 | 세션 설정의 폴더 | `… 세션 폴더를 엽니다 · <경로>` |

스냅샷의 창별 폴더가 아니라 셸의 실시간 값을 먼저 보는 이유는 나눈 자리의 터미널이 폴더를 물려받을 때와 같다 — 스냅샷은 명령이 오갈 때만 갱신돼 그 사이의 `cd` 를 놓친다.

**폴더 문자열은 화면 속 프로그램이 정할 수 있다.** 창별 폴더는 셸이 `OSC 9;9` 로 스스로 알린 값인데 그 바이트를 찍을 수 있는 것은 셸만이 아니다(`cat evil.bin`). 그래서 하이퍼링크를 열 때와 같은 자세로 막는다(`commands/reveal.rs`).

- **폴더만** 넘긴다 — `explorer.exe <파일>` 은 그 파일을 기본 처리기로 **여는** 것이라 `.exe`·`.lnk` 하나면 그대로 실행이다. `/select,…`·`shell:startup` 같은 것도 폴더가 아니라 함께 걸린다.
- **네트워크 경로(UNC)는 열지 않는다** — 윈도우가 그 호스트에 붙으며 NTLM 을 흘린다. 존재를 확인하는 것만으로도 붙으러 가므로 파일 시스템을 만지기 **전에** 거른다.
- 제어문자·방향 전환 문자, 상대 경로(윈도우에서는 WSL 의 `/home/…` 이 여기서 걸린다), 없는 폴더는 다음 후보로 물러난다. 셸은 거치지 않고 `explorer.exe` 에 argv 하나로 넘긴다.

## 2. 한글을 치다 `Shift+Enter` — 마지막 글자가 다음 줄로 밀리던 것

조합 중인 음절은 xterm 이 `compositionend` 자리에서 곧바로 보내지 않고 **한 틱 뒤에** 보낸다(`CompositionHelper._finalizeComposition` 의 `setTimeout(…, 0)`). 브라우저가 조합이 끝난 **뒤에** 밀어 넣는 `input` 이벤트까지 봐야 확정된 글자를 알 수 있기 때문이다. 그 틈에 줄바꿈을 그 자리에서 써 버려 아직 나가지 않은 음절을 앞질렀다 — `claude`·`codex` 에서 보이던 자리다.

이제 조합의 시작과 끝을 따라가다가(`compositionstart`·`compositionend`) 그 사이에 눌린 줄바꿈은 붙잡아 두고, 글자가 나간 **뒤에** 보낸다. 우리 `compositionend` 처리기는 xterm 것보다 나중에 붙으므로 거기서 잡는 `setTimeout(…, 0)` 도 xterm 이 먼저 잡아 둔 것 뒤에 놓인다 — 음절이 먼저, 줄바꿈이 뒤.

키 이벤트의 `isComposing` 만 보는 것으로는 모자라다. 크로미움은 IME 가 음절을 확정하며 넘긴 `Enter` 를 `compositionend` **뒤에** 주기도 하는데(그때 `isComposing` 은 이미 거짓이다), 그 순간에도 글자는 여전히 그 `setTimeout` 안에 남아 있다. 그래서 "조합이 끝나기를 기다리는 중" 까지를 줄바꿈을 미룰 자리로 본다. 보내는 바이트는 그대로다(win32-input-mode 면 `Ctrl+J` 키 이벤트, 아니면 순수 LF).

## 테스트

```
cd src-tauri && cargo test --workspace   # 138개 (reveal 경로 검사 7개 추가)
pnpm test                                # 382개 (한글 조합 줄바꿈 5개 · 탐색기 메뉴 2개 추가)
pnpm build                               # tsc --noEmit + vite build
```

순서를 보는 새 테스트 3개는 고치기 전 코드에서 실제로 실패하는 것을 확인했다(줄바꿈이 음절보다 먼저 나간다).
